# How to Turn ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Transcripts Into Notes and Tasks

> **In short:** Upload a recording to ElevenLabs Scribe v3 to get a written transcript, then use an AI chat assistant to turn that text into a recap, an action list, and a follow-up email. Check that everyone agreed to be recorded, and review every name and date yourself.

A recording is only useful if you can find the important parts later. In this guide you'll turn a meeting or call into three things: a short recap, a checklist of who owes what, and a follow-up email. Along the way you'll learn a workflow that goes beyond a single question, where each step builds on the one before. It's written for anyone who handles meetings at work, plans things with family, or keeps track of school or volunteer groups.

## Before you start
- An ElevenLabs account and access to the Scribe v3 transcription feature. It may require a paid plan or usage credits, so check the official pricing page, because plans change.
- A recording of a meeting or call you are allowed to use, saved as an audio or video file on your phone or computer.
- An AI chat assistant you already use. This guide assumes you can sign in and send a message.
- About 30 to 40 minutes, depending on how long your recording is.

## Step 1 — Check permission and prepare the recording
Before you upload anything, make sure everyone in the recording knows it is being made and has agreed to it. Recording rules differ by place and by workplace, so if you're unsure, ask your manager or a professional rather than relying on this guide. Next, find your file in its folder. Short clips are easier to check, so if your recording is long, consider trimming it into parts by time using a basic audio editor or your phone's recording app. Look for a trim or split option. If you can't find one, you can still upload the full file.

You'll know it worked when you can play the file and hear the whole conversation from start to finish.

## Step 2 — Upload the file and start the transcription
Sign in to ElevenLabs and look for a section about speech-to-text or transcription. "Scribe" is the name of the model that turns spoken words into written text. Look for an upload button or a box where you can drag and drop your file. Choose your recording and start the transcription. Processing usually takes a while, and longer files take more time. When it finishes, a text version appears on the screen.

If the options look different, look for a model choice and select Scribe v3 if you see it. If you can't find the transcription area at all, search the site's help or use its search feature for "speech to text." Keep in mind that the transcript is only a text record of the words spoken. It can't tell you what was important or who owes what.

You'll know it worked when the text on the screen matches the words you heard in the recording.

## Step 3 — Clean up the transcript
Read the transcript while listening to the recording at a few key moments, especially where names, numbers, and dates appear. ElevenLabs says, according to its own announcement, that Scribe v3 has 27% fewer word errors than Scribe v2. That's the company's claim, and it doesn't mean the text is perfect. Unusual names, product codes, and people talking over each other are the places most likely to be wrong.

Next, check who said what. The company's announcement says its real-time version, Scribe v3 Live, adds speaker labels. For a recorded file, check whether your output already shows speakers. If it doesn't, add simple labels yourself, such as "Speaker 1" or a first name, at the start of each turn. Fix the errors you find and save a clean copy.

You'll know it worked when the names, numbers, and dates in your text match the recording, and each speaker is labeled clearly enough to follow.

## Step 4 — Ask an AI assistant for a recap
Open your AI chat assistant and start a new chat. Paste your cleaned transcript into the message box at the bottom and write your instructions above it. Put the instructions first, so the assistant knows what to do with the text. Send the message and wait for the response, which appears below your message. For long transcripts, the reply can take a moment.

💬 Example: "Write a meeting recap in five bullet points for [meeting topic]. Use only what the transcript says, and write UNCLEAR next to anything you cannot tell. Here is the transcript: [paste transcript here]."

If the text is too long for one message, split the transcript into two parts, send the first part with the instructions, and ask the assistant to wait for the second part before writing the recap.

You'll know it worked when the recap covers the main decisions and stays close to what was actually said.

## Step 5 — Build an action list from the same chat
Stay in the same chat so the assistant still has the transcript in front of it. Ask for a checklist of tasks, with the owner and due date for each one. Many chats keep earlier messages, but very long conversations can cause the assistant to lose track of early details. If the answer seems to forget something, paste the transcript again. The assistant can't know what was meant if nobody said it, so ask it to say "not stated" instead of guessing.

💬 Example: "From the transcript above, list every action item as a checkbox line with the owner and due date. If no owner or date was said, write not stated instead of guessing."

When the list appears, compare each line with the recording. Cross out anything that wasn't really agreed on, and add any task the assistant missed.

You'll know it worked when every task on the list matches something you can find in the recording.

## Step 6 — Draft the follow-up email
Ask the same chat to combine your recap and action list into a short email. Tell it who the email is for, how long it should be, and what you want readers to do next. A clear request at the end, like asking people to reply by a date, makes the email easier to act on. Read the draft slowly. Assistants sometimes add small details that weren't in the meeting, so remove anything you can't confirm, then copy the text into your email app and send it yourself.

💬 Example: "Using the recap and action list above, write a friendly follow-up email to [team name] under 150 words. Include the three most important tasks and ask anyone with a question to reply by [date]."

If the email sounds too formal or too casual, ask for a second version with a different tone, such as "a little warmer" or "more direct." Then pick the one that sounds like you.

You'll know it worked when the email is short, names only people who appeared in the recording, and you've edited it into your own words.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting the transcript without checking it.** Speech-to-text can mishear names and numbers. Fix it by listening to the recording at the key moments before you share anything.
- **Recording people without asking first.** Consent rules differ, and it's easy to forget. Fix it by telling everyone at the start that the call is being recorded, and by checking your workplace policy.
- **Pasting sensitive details into a chat without thinking.** A transcript can include private information about people. Fix it by removing personal or confidential details you aren't allowed to share before pasting, and by only using tools your workplace approves.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A family planning call or a school parent meeting can become a short note of what was agreed, with a list of who is doing what by when.
- **For your business or work:** A meeting recap and a list of action items can go out within an hour, instead of someone rewriting notes from memory.
- **If you want to go further:** Save your recap instructions in one place so every recap uses the same format. If your AI assistant offers a way to save instructions, such as a project or a custom instructions setting, put your prompt there and test it on a second recording.

This workflow can't replace listening to the recording yourself, and it can't know decisions that nobody said out loud. It's a faster way to get organized, and you're still the one who checks the results.

## Try it now
Pick a short recording you have permission to use, upload it to ElevenLabs Scribe v3, and paste the transcript into your AI chat assistant. Ask for a three-bullet summary, then check it against the audio. In about two minutes, you'll have seen the whole workflow work once.
